title: The Tax Agent Who Found A Forgotten Ledger: How One Notebook Took Down Al Capone

beats.text: Chicago, 1930. Late at night, a federal tax agent named Frank Wilson is digging through an old storage room.
He has spent months trying to prove one thing. That the most famous gangster in America has an income.
It sounds easy. Everyone knows Al Capone is rich. But on paper, he owns almost nothing.
No bank account in his name. No property. No signed cheques. Everything paid in cash, through other people.
Then, the story goes, Wilson finds a package of old files nobody had looked at in years.
Inside is a set of black ledgers. And in the columns of money, a name. Just two letters. Al.
That notebook will do what bullets, raids and murder trials never could. It will put Al Capone in prison.
To understand why a notebook mattered, you have to understand how untouchable Capone was.
Prohibition had made alcohol illegal across America in 1920. And illegal alcohol made gangs very, very rich.
By the late 1920s, Capone ran a huge network of breweries, speakeasies, gambling halls and protection rackets around Chicago.
Estimates of his income ran into the tens of millions of dollars a year. Nobody could prove a single cent.
Police were paid off. Witnesses vanished or forgot what they saw. Murder cases went nowhere.
In 1929, seven men were shot dead in a garage on Valentine's Day. The public blamed Capone, but he was never charged.

beats.text: By 1930, the Chicago Crime Commission had named him Public Enemy Number One. And Washington wanted him gone.
President Herbert Hoover, the story goes, kept asking his Treasury Secretary the same question. Have you got that fellow Capone yet?
The answer came from a Supreme Court ruling most people have never heard of.
In 1927, in a case about a bootlegger named Manley Sullivan, the court said income from crime is still income. And it can be taxed.
A bootlegger could not refuse to file a tax return just because the money was illegal.
So the government changed its plan. Forget proving murder. Prove he earned money, and never paid tax on it.
The job went to a small team in the Treasury's Special Intelligence Unit, led by Elmer Irey.
They tried it first on the people around him. In 1930, Capone's brother Ralph was convicted of tax evasion. So was the gang's money man, Jake Guzik.
Now they wanted the boss. And the agent on his trail was Frank Wilson.
Wilson was not a gunfighter. He was a careful, quiet investigator who read bank records the way detectives read crime scenes.
He went through bank deposits, property records, phone bills and hotel bills, looking for any money with Capone's fingerprints on it.
He found spending. Expensive suits, fine furniture, a mansion in Florida. But the money was always in someone else's name.
Months went by. Some in Washington began to think the case could never be made.
Then came that night in the storage room.
The ledgers had been seized years earlier, in a 1926 raid on a gambling house in Cicero called the Hawthorne Smoke Shop.
It was one of the gang's biggest casinos. After the raid, the books were simply filed away.
Wilson saw what nobody else had seen. Page after page of daily profits, most of it written in one neat hand.
Over about three years, the books showed profits of more than half a million dollars, and money being split between partners, including someone called Al.
But a notebook proves nothing on its own. A jury would ask one question. Who wrote it?
So Wilson did something painstaking. He started collecting handwriting.
Bank deposit slips. Voter registration cards. Bail bond papers. Anything a Capone man might have signed.
For weeks, he compared letters and loops, page by page, against the writing in the ledger.
Then he found a match. A deposit slip written by a man named Leslie Shumway.
Shumway had worked as a bookkeeper at the Hawthorne Smoke Shop. And he had left Chicago.
Agents tracked him to Miami, where, accounts say, he was working at a dog track.
Shumway was terrified. Testifying against Capone could get him killed. But the choice was simple. Help the government, or face charges himself.
He agreed to testify. The government kept him hidden and guarded until the trial.
A second cashier, Fred Ries, was also found and pressured into talking about where the money went.
In June 1931, a federal grand jury indicted Al Capone for income tax evasion.
Capone's lawyers made a deal. He would plead guilty, and in return he expected a light sentence, about two and a half years.
But Judge James Wilkerson refused to be bound by it. Capone withdrew his plea. Now there would be a trial.
On the first day, in October 1931, there was one more surprise. The judge swapped the entire jury with the panel from another courtroom.
He had been warned that Capone's men might have reached the original jurors. With the switch, any bribes were wasted.
In court, Shumway took the stand and explained the books, line by line.
The defence argued Capone was a gambler who lost as much as he won. The jury did not buy it.
On the eighteenth of October, 1931, the verdict came in. Guilty on five counts of tax crimes.
The sentence was eleven years, one of the longest ever given for tax crimes at the time, plus heavy fines and costs.
Now here is the part most people get wrong. Ask who took down Al Capone, and most people will say Eliot Ness.
Ness and his team, the Untouchables, were real. They raided breweries and cost the gang a fortune.
But the Prohibition charges built from that work were never tried. It was the tax case that sent Capone to prison.
The man who really caught Capone was a quiet accountant with a ledger, a pile of deposit slips and a lot of patience.
Capone went to the federal prison in Atlanta in 1932. In 1934 he was moved to the new island prison of Alcatraz.
There, the most powerful man in Chicago was just another prisoner. His empire moved on without him.
Already ill with a disease he had caught years earlier, he was released in 1939, his mind failing.
He died at his Florida home in January 1947. He was forty-eight.
Frank Wilson went on to become chief of the US Secret Service.
And his method became a rule that still catches criminals today. When you cannot prove the crime, follow the money.
Capone survived gunfights, raids and murder investigations. What he could not survive was his own bookkeeping.
